title: Bacterial production of AAV and lentiviral gene therapy vectors

concept.text: Millennium Problems for Biology 7, Bacterial production of gene therapies. Target: infectious, replication-incompetent AAV and lentivirus produced in bacteria, with a prespecified genome, capsid and infectious-unit ratios similar to mammalian-cell production, and nuclease-resistant genomes; AAV alone counts as partial success. Sources given: https://millenniumproblems.bio/.

change_log.change: Added by hand to GEN on 2026-11-15.
change_log.reason: One of the twelve Millennium Problems for Biology (Sam Rodriques and Michaela Hinks, FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, 2026), each with a stated concrete target; added at the owner's request, November 14, 2026.

page.title: Bacterial production of AAV and lentiviral vectors
page.definition: Bacteria produce adeno-associated virus (AAV) and lentiviral vectors: gene-delivery particles that enter target cells but cannot independently propagate. Their specified genomes resist nuclease digestion, and their particle and infectivity ratios meet the published comparisons with mammalian-cell preparations.

goal.need: A 2025 assessment by Dream and Odum describes an illustrative systemic AAV manufacturing run yielding approximately 10 doses per batch at nearly US$100,000 in manufacturing cost per dose. These estimates quantify the manufacturing constraint motivating investigation of alternative vector-production platforms.

figures.caption: Illustrative systemic AAV manufacturing run described in a 2025 assessment
figures.note: Author estimates for the example described, rather than measurements from bacterial production.

completion.title: Bacteria produce infectious, replication-incompetent AAV and lentivirus meeting mammalian vector benchmarks.
completion.criterion: Produce both infectious, replication-incompetent AAV and lentivirus in bacteria. Each contains a prespecified viral genome protected from nucleases. For each, physical capsids per viral genome and infectious units per viral genome must be similar to those obtained from purified mammalian-cell preparations. The specification provides no numerical tolerance for similarity.
completion.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, The Millennium Problems for Biology, Problem 7, published challenge-validation specification.
completion.threshold_quote: replication-incompetent AAV and lentivirus in bacteria.
completion.basis: This is Problem 7's success test. Its AAV-only partial-success clause makes both classes necessary for completion. FDA separately recognises particle and infectivity ratios as quality attributes, with acceptance criteria justified for individual products.

milestones.title: Vector structural proteins made in bacteria assemble into virus-like particles.
milestones.criterion: Bacterially expressed vector structural proteins form virus-like particles, with assembly established by structural and capsid-specific evidence. Le et al. reported cell-free AAV2 assembly on 9 December 2019 (approximately 22 nm; AFM size comparison n=9 particles), followed by AAV5 assembly inside E. coli on 24 October 2022. These peer-reviewed results establish particle assembly without demonstrating delivery of a vector genome.
milestones.set_by: AAV virus-like-particle research convention, exemplified by Le et al. (2019, 2022). The cited assembly evidence was established for AAV.
milestones.threshold_quote: We generated these empty capsids by bacterial expression and subsequent concomitant protein refolding and VLP formation.

milestones.title: Bacterial vector particles contain a prespecified genome that resists nuclease digestion.
milestones.criterion: Particles produced in bacteria contain the prespecified genome in a nuclease-resistant form. Le's 2021 dissertation reports DNA protection by cell-free AAV5-like particles but no reporter expression in CHO-K1 cells (replicate count unstated; not journal peer reviewed). An unreviewed master's thesis abstract deposited on 30 January 2026 reports genome-containing hybrid AAV-based particles made in bacteria; its embargo prevents verification of nuclease protection.
milestones.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, Problem 7's genome-content and nuclease-resistance requirements, specified for both vector classes.

milestones.title: One bacterial vector class is replication-incompetent and meets the mammalian vector-ratio comparisons.
milestones.criterion: For one vector class, bacteria produce infectious, replication-incompetent particles containing a prespecified, nuclease-resistant genome, with capsid/genome and infectious-unit/genome ratios similar to mammalian preparations. The challenge explicitly recognises AAV alone as partial success.
milestones.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, Problem 7. The partial-success clause is written for AAV alone; the full-success clause specifies the per-vector requirements for both classes.
milestones.threshold_quote: AAV on its own will be considered a partial success.

not_found: No numerical equivalence margin for Problem 7's mammalian-production comparisons was found in the challenge, FDA guidance or NIST programme documents.
Searches for bacterial AAV and lentiviral production found no verified fulfilment of either the AAV-only partial-success test or the full challenge.
Hosseinali's embargoed thesis full text could not be opened; its abstract supplies no sample counts or infectivity-comparison results.
Biological replicate counts for the assembly observations and dissertation genome-protection experiment were not established from the opened accounts.
No regulator, society or standards-body roadmap specifying stages for bacterial production of these two vector classes was found.

results.finding: AAV5 VP3 proteins formed virus-like particles in E. coli; sample size not reported.
results.detail: Assembly was supported by atomic force microscopy and ELISA using an intact-capsid antibody and an AAVR domain.
results.quote: VP3 capsid proteins of AAV serotype 5 (AAV5) were expressed, and VLPs were readily purified. The correct assembly was confirmed by ELISA with an intact-capsid AAV5 antibody and an AAVR domain as well as by atomic force microscopy.

results.finding: E. coli cell-free-produced AAV5 VP3 particles measured 19.6 ± 1.8 nm by TEM (n=80 particles).
results.detail: TEM provided structural evidence, and an AAV5-specific ELISA detected assembled capsids.

results.finding: HIV-1 Gag expressed in E. coli formed spherical particles at 37 °C; sample size not stated.
results.detail: Electron microscopy showed spherical particles, and Gag assembled into high-order multimers comparable to virus-like particles produced in eukaryotic cells.
results.quote: When E. coli expression was performed at 37 degrees C, Gag predominantly assembled to a high order of multimer, apparently equivalent to the virus-like particles obtained following Gag expression in eukaryotic cells, through the formation of low orders of multimer characterized with a discreet sedimentation value of 60 S.
